Fetal Echo Project · Unit D8 · Detect tier · v0.1

Rate and rhythm for the screener

DRAFT - NOT FOR CLINICAL USE. Contains claims with status 'ai-extracted' that no clinician has verified.

You will be able to

  • Give the normal fetal heart rate at screening.
  • State when ectopic beats or an irregular rhythm need further assessment.
  • Tell transient slowing from persistent bradycardia, and transient speeding from persistent tachycardia.
  • Name the rhythm findings that are indications for fetal echocardiography.
  • Describe in outline how a specialist works out the mechanism of an arrhythmia.

Normal

The normal heart rate is 120 to 160 beats per minute, and the rhythm should be regular.1

The screener's task is not to name the arrhythmia. It is to recognise the findings that the guideline lists as needing further assessment. The guideline does not give a rule for every pattern in between; see the missing claims for this unit.

The irregular beat

Ectopic beats, seen as skipped beats, are the most common rhythm disturbance. They are often benign and resolve on their own. In low-risk populations they are not linked to a higher risk of structural heart disease.2

Further assessment is indicated when ectopic episodes are frequent, meaning more often than every three to five beats, or when the rhythm stays irregular for more than one to two weeks.3

The slow heart

Transient bradycardia is seen in normal second-trimester fetuses and is associated with pressure from the transducer.4

A rate that stays at 110 beats per minute or below in a fetus that is otherwise well needs timely evaluation by a fetal cardiac specialist. Possible causes include frequent blocked atrial ectopic beats, atrioventricular block and sinus bradycardia.4

Recurrent decelerations of the fetal heart rate in the third trimester can reflect fetal hypoxia.5

The fast heart

A mild, brief rise to 160 to 180 beats per minute can be a normal variant during fetal movement.6

A rate that stays at 180 beats per minute or above should be evaluated further for a tachyarrhythmia or fetal hypoxia.6

At a glance

Rate and rhythm findings and what each means at screening.1,2,3,4,6

FindingMeaning for the screener
120 to 160 per minute, regularNormal
Occasional skipped beatsThe most common rhythm disturbance; often benign
Skipped beats more often than every three to five beats, or irregular for more than one to two weeksFurther assessment
Transient slowing, associated with probe pressure, in the second trimesterSeen in normal fetuses
Stays at 110 per minute or below in a well fetusTimely specialist evaluation
Brief rise to 160 to 180 per minute with movementCan be a normal variant
Stays at 180 per minute or aboveFurther evaluation

Rhythm findings that are indications for fetal echocardiography

The guideline lists these among the fetal indications for fetal echocardiography: persistent tachycardia at 180 beats per minute or more, suspected heart block or persistent bradycardia at 110 or less, and a rhythm that is frequently or persistently irregular.7

How the echocardiography guideline words it

The echocardiography guideline describes a sustained rate below 120 beats per minute as abnormal at any gestation, and a sustained rate above 160 to 180 as abnormal. The screening guideline sets its thresholds for referral at 110 or less and 180 or more. This unit teaches the screening thresholds.8,9,4,6

What the specialist will do

Every fetal echocardiogram must document the heart rate and rhythm.10

Repeated blocked premature atrial beats can look like second- or third-degree heart block and must be told apart from it.11

When the rhythm is irregular, slow or fast, the mechanism should be documented with M-mode, pulsed-wave Doppler or tissue Doppler, alone or together.12

M-mode times the atria against the ventricles: the cursor passes through an atrial wall and the free wall of a ventricle together.13

Pulsed-wave Doppler does the same by sampling two flows at once: superior vena cava with ascending aorta, mitral inflow with aortic outflow, or pulmonary artery with pulmonary vein.14

Knowing what these techniques are helps you explain to the family why they are being referred.

Rate and rhythm at every screen

  • Rate between 120 and 160 per minute1
  • Rhythm regular1
  • Rate stays at 110 or below in a well fetus: timely specialist evaluation arranged4
  • Persistent rate of 180 or above: further evaluation arranged6
  • Ectopic beats more often than every three to five beats: further assessment arranged3
  • Rhythm irregular for more than one to two weeks: further assessment arranged3

Still to be written

  • How urgently each rhythm finding should be seen (same day, within a week) - not stated in the screening guideline; needs a source and the editor's decision.
  • Signs that a fetus with an arrhythmia is unwell (hydrops, effusions) and what the screener should record - needs a source.
  • How to count the fetal heart rate reliably at screening (M-mode or Doppler method) - needs a source.
  • What to do with patterns the guideline does not grade (for example a rate between 110 and 120, or occasional ectopic beats at a single visit): a complete triage scheme needs a source or the editor's teaching.
  • Maternal conditions linked to heart block and how they change follow-up - planned for XC4.
